claims.summary: Registry — The registry is the overall store and can host many repositories; choose it when identifying the top-level resource, not one named image family.
Repository — The storage unit defines a repository as images with the same name and different tags, which is the collection requested.
Manifest — A manifest describes an individual artifact’s layers and configuration; it fits inspecting that artifact rather than grouping its versions.

Pin the original base-image digest in every Dockerfile. — A digest is appropriate for a frozen reproducible input. Here the input must advance to compatible patched content, so fixing the original digest defeats servicing.

Use a never-reused tag for the original base-image build. — A never-reused tag identifies a fixed build and is useful for controlled production deployment. It does not advance the tracked input to later patches.

Use a stable release-line tag and update it with compatible patches. — The versioning unit recommends stable tags for serviced bases; the tasks unit supplies same-registry base-update triggering. The already-tracked mutable input can advance without editing the Dockerfile.

Use only the application commit hash. — A commit identifies source state and is useful for source lookup. Rebuilding that commit after base changes can produce separate executions, so it is not the required execution identity.

Use the system name and its build number as a delimited pair, never reusing the pair. — The source supports combined identifiers and build traceability. Given the stated local uniqueness, adding the system namespace makes each producing execution distinct; never reusing the tag preserves that assignment.
Use only the local build number. — The number identifies an execution within one system. It would suffice in a single numbering namespace, but the two systems can independently issue the same number.

Reuse one semantic release-line tag after successful builds. — Stable release-line aliases suit consumers intentionally following updates. They do not preserve a never-reused identifier for each producing execution.
A manifest lists an image’s layers and configuration. — The storage unit directly describes this manifest role. It concerns artifact composition, not the repository collection tested by c001.
A manifest groups differently tagged versions under one image name. — This is the repository role. It is appropriate when describing the named collection, not a manifest for an individual artifact.

Images can share identical content-addressed layers. — The storage unit describes shared common layers and content-addressed identification, so separate images need not store separate copies of identical layers.
A layer is the human-readable alias that can move to another image. — This describes a tag. Tags can move between image manifests; a layer represents content rather than a mutable alias.
An additional semantic-version tag — An additional tag is an alias useful for version communication. It does not set the documented write-enabled control.
The digest in the release record — Recording a digest provides traceability and exact content identity. It is not a registry-side mutation of the deployed tag’s write attribute.

The deployed tag’s write-enabled attribute to false — The versioning unit demonstrates az acr repository update with --image and --write-enabled false for deployed-image write locking. The claim is limited to the write safeguard.
latest — The storage and versioning units specify latest as the omitted-tag default. It is a name, not a calculation of the newest semantic version.
5.0 — This named version can be requested explicitly with :5.0. Docker does not choose it merely because it is the largest version-shaped tag.
4.2 — This named version can be requested explicitly with :4.2. An omitted tag does not select that historical version.
az acr run — The tasks unit uses run to execute a command in an existing image. That is useful for a smoke test but does not perform the source build requested here.
az acr task logs — Task logs retrieve build execution output. They are useful for diagnosing an existing run rather than starting a source build.
az acr build — The tasks unit describes a quick build that uploads the context, builds in Azure and pushes the image, without a local Docker engine.
The local working directory, using . — The local-directory context uploads the files presently on disk, including the two uncommitted edits supplied in the scenario.
The remote branch URL — A Git context builds content available at the chosen remote location. It is appropriate after the desired edits reach that branch, not before.
The published remote tarball URL — A remote tarball is a supported context for the content in that archive. The stipulated archive predates both edits, so it tests the wrong input snapshot.

Move frequently changing Dockerfile instructions later. — Instruction ordering can improve layer-cache reuse during the build. It does not exclude the unused recordings from the uploaded source context.

Exclude the recordings folder with .dockerignore. — The tasks unit recommends .dockerignore to remove unnecessary context files and reduce upload size. The stated unused folder can be excluded without changing required inputs.
Add the task run ID to the output image tag. — A run-ID tag improves build traceability. It does not reduce the source context or the measured upload time.

Enable container continuous deployment and configure ACR push events to call the returned webhook. — The deployment unit describes continuous deployment returning a webhook and a registry push-event webhook triggering restart so App Service pulls updated content. Both sides of the integration are needed.

Update the web app to a different unique image tag for every release. — Changing the configured image tag triggers a restart and is appropriate for explicit releases. It does not preserve the stipulated same-tag, push-driven development workflow.

Restart the web app manually after the present push. — A restart causes App Service to check the image and pull changed layers, repairing this one deployment. It does not arrange automatic pickup of future pushes.

Change LOG_LEVEL to DEBUG and retain WEBSITES_PORT=8000. — A debug log level can help collect application evidence when needed, but it does not change the forwarding destination. The actual listener is already known.

Change registry credentials and retain WEBSITES_PORT=8000. — Registry credentials address failed image pulls. The image has pulled successfully, so this leaves the demonstrated forwarding mismatch unchanged.
Change WEBSITES_PORT to 7000. — The runtime unit documents WEBSITES_PORT for a nondefault listener. Setting it to the observed port aligns App Service forwarding without rebuilding the container.

Set the web app startup command to --mode batch. — The runtime unit states that the App Service startup command replaces CMD while retaining ENTRYPOINT. Under this supplied dispatcher contract the new arguments select batch mode.

Add an app setting named MODE with value batch. — App settings inject environment variables and are appropriate when the application reads them. This dispatcher explicitly does not read a mode variable.
Rebuild the image with CMD set to --mode batch. — Changing the Dockerfile default is appropriate when publishing a new image with new default behavior. Here the image must remain unchanged.
CUSTOMCONNSTR_Reporting — The Custom connection-string type receives CUSTOMCONNSTR_. This would match a Custom entry, not the stated SQLAzure type.
Reporting — An ordinary app setting named Reporting is injected under that name. The scenario instead supplies a typed connection string.
SQLAZURECONNSTR_Reporting — The settings unit’s prefix table maps SQL Azure connection strings to SQLAZURECONNSTR_, followed by the configured name.
SQLCONNSTR_Reporting — SQLCONNSTR_ corresponds to SQL Server connection strings. It is a valid different type mapping, not the SQLAzure mapping shown.

The secret’s ordinary HTTPS URI as a literal value. — A literal URI is useful for an application that consumes a URI and fetches the secret itself. This unchanged application expects the secret value, and an ordinary URI does not request App Service resolution.

An @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) reference to the secret. — The settings unit describes this reference syntax and managed-identity prerequisites. App Service resolves the reference and supplies the secret value through the existing environment variable.

The current secret value entered directly as an encrypted-at-rest app setting. — App settings can hold runtime values and are encrypted at rest. Direct entry can suit app-managed configuration, but it copies the current value and does not use the required Key Vault reference mechanism.

Enable App Service storage and keep writing reports to /app/output. — Enabling storage mounts the persistent /home location. It is sufficient only if the application writes into that mount; retaining the unrelated path leaves these reports outside it.

Keep storage disabled and change the output path to /home/output. — The /home path is useful for persisted output when the App Service storage mount is enabled. A path name alone does not enable the disabled persistent-storage feature.

Enable App Service storage and write reports to /home/output. — The runtime unit documents WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE=true and persistence/shared content under /home. Both enabling the mount and choosing a path in it are required here.

The Kudu Environment page — This page verifies applied environment variables. It has already supplied that evidence and does not provide a view of the application container’s running processes or full filesystem.

An SSH session into the running application container — The diagnostics unit distinguishes the SCM site from the application container and directs in-container filesystem/process inspection to SSH when the image supports it.
The Kudu mounted-storage file browser — This browser is useful for mounted paths such as /home and /home/LogFiles. It is not a browser for the complete image filesystem or its running processes.

Place the production API and worker in separate environments, retaining internal-only worker ingress. — Separate environments fit independent network/lifecycle groups. Internal ingress is scoped to the worker’s environment, so this does not give the stipulated API its same-environment access.

Place production and development in one environment under different app names. — Different app names distinguish resources within a shared environment. They suit related services sharing that boundary, not the requested separate development lifecycle and logging setup.

Place the production services together with internal worker ingress, and development in a different environment. — The environment unit aligns privately communicating services with a shared environment and recommends lifecycle separation for development versus production.

Change the container image reference in properties.template. — The revision-modes unit explicitly lists images and template properties as revision-scope changes. The updated image belongs to a new immutable revision.

Change an existing secret value in properties.configuration. — Secrets are application-scope changes in the revision-modes unit. This is appropriate for changing the stored secret, not for creating a new template revision.
Change ingress traffic-splitting weights. — Traffic splitting is application-scoped; changing weights routes among revisions without itself creating a new template snapshot.
Change the scale rules in properties.template. — The revision-modes unit explicitly lists scale rules as revision-scoped changes. A new scaling template therefore produces a new revision.

Keep serving from the existing revision while the replacement becomes ready. — The revision-modes unit says single mode keeps the existing revision serving while the replacement starts and waits for health/readiness before handoff. Provisioning alone is not that readiness condition.

Shift traffic to the replacement after its health checks pass and the readiness transition completes. — This is the documented subsequent handoff when the replacement is ready. Those conditions are not yet true, so it does not describe the current interval.

Distribute traffic across concurrently active revisions using configured canary weights. — Configured canary splitting is appropriate in multiple revision mode with ready revisions. The stipulated single-mode transition does not use that operator-managed split.

Increase v2’s application-URL traffic weight to 100%. — Changing weights directs ordinary application traffic and is useful for completing a rollout. It violates the unchanged production-weight requirement and does not provide a separate tester endpoint.

Assign an ordinary revision label to v2 and use its label URL. — The revision-modes unit states that label URLs route to the labeled revision independently of application traffic weights and labels can move between revisions.
Keep using the application URL with its existing 90/10 split. — That URL is appropriate for a production canary experiment sampling both revisions. It cannot give these testers dedicated v2 access.
Eight replicas — Forty messages divided by the five-message target requests eight before applying bounds. Eight would be allowed with a maximum of at least eight, but the shown maximum is six.

Five replicas — Five could be the desired count for 25 messages at this target when no other bound intervenes. The message target is not itself a desired replica count for the supplied 40-message backlog.
Six replicas — The KEDA unit defines message-count divided by target, producing eight here. The configured maximum in the scale rules limits the requested ceiling to six.

Map the scaler’s connection parameter to the existing bus-connection secret. — The KEDA unit maps a scaler authentication parameter to a Container Apps secret. Repairing that missing reference supplies the existing credential to the scaler, separately from application use.

Reconfigure the registry identity used for image pulls. — Registry identity configuration is relevant when image pulls fail. Pulls already work here and registry configuration does not replace the scaler’s event-source authentication reference.

Set the worker’s runtime connection-string environment variable again. — Runtime secret references configure the application process. They are appropriate for a broken application credential lookup, but this process already reads messages and the scaler has its own failed reference.

Edit the image value inside the YAML and apply that file. — The deployment unit states that --yaml makes the file the configuration source and other configuration flags are ignored. Updating the reviewed file changes the authoritative image value.

Change only the --image argument while retaining the old YAML image. — The image flag updates an image in a flag-based update without YAML. It does not override the image supplied by the authoritative YAML file in this flow.

Remove --yaml and deploy using only the --image argument. — A flag-based image update is supported and can change the live image. It abandons the required reviewed-YAML source of truth rather than fixing that file.

{"name":"API_KEY","value":"provider-key"} — A value field supplies an ordinary literal environment string. This is useful when an application expects a nonsensitive identifier, not when it expects the secret’s contents.

{"name":"API_KEY","secretRef":"provider-key"} — The runtime unit’s template example uses secretRef with the existing secret name. The CLI secretref: notation belongs to CLI environment arguments, not a template literal value.

{"name":"API_KEY","secretRef":"backup-key"} — This is a valid template reference to the existing test-provider secret. It is appropriate for that provider, but the production application explicitly requires provider-key instead.

Set an application environment variable containing the registry server name. — Environment variables are consumed by the application after startup. A server-name setting can configure application behavior but does not select Container Apps registry authentication.

Replace the registry password with another valid password. — Username/password authentication is documented for private registries and can repair bad credentials. It keeps the stored-credential mode that this deployment must replace.

Update the ACR registry entry with --identity system. — The registry unit explicitly demonstrates az containerapp registry set --server with --identity system after identity assignment and pull permission. This selects the desired pull authentication method.

A: system logs; B: application console logs. — The verification unit separates platform system logs from container console output. A platform pull failure is investigated in system evidence; B’s application exception belongs to stdout/stderr console evidence.

A: application console logs; B: system logs. — Console logs are useful once application code runs, while system logs help platform lifecycle failures. This swaps those roles for the stated stages and may leave A with no application output.

A: replica count; B: ingress FQDN. — Replica status and ingress FQDN help identify whether instances exist and how to reach them. They are useful deployment checks but do not contain the pull error or the application exception details requested.
queueName=documents on the Service Bus scaler — queueName selects a Service Bus queue. It is appropriate for a queue named documents, but the stated work is in a topic subscription.

topicName=documents and subscriptionName=enrich on the Service Bus scaler — The KEDA unit says to replace queueName with topicName plus subscriptionName for subscriptions, which maintain independent active-message counts.

topicName=documents and subscriptionName=audit on the Service Bus scaler — This correctly identifies the audit subscriber’s backlog. It is useful for that separate consumer but would scale enrich from the wrong pending work.

During: 7; later: 3 — Seven is the cron request and would dominate if the HTTP request were at most seven. Here HTTP requests eleven, so treating cron as an overriding fixed count misses the highest-request rule.
During: 9; later: 2 — Nine correctly caps the active-window request. A later count of two would fit demand at or below the minimum, but the remaining HTTP rule requests three.

During: 9; later: 3 — The custom-scaler unit combines rules using the highest request. Eleven dominates seven and is capped at nine; outside the cron window only HTTP requests three, which lies between the minimum and maximum.

Raising maxReplicas alone cannot add more simultaneous partition readers to this consumer group. — The KEDA unit states that one consumer per partition operates within a consumer group. With all four partitions already assigned, extra replicas cannot create additional partition-reader concurrency.

Raising maxReplicas from four to twelve adds eight effective partition readers. — A higher replica bound can enable more partition readers when enough unassigned partitions exist. The fixed four-partition group does not have those additional assignments.

Lowering the lag threshold creates more concurrently readable partitions. — A lower metric threshold can request replicas sooner while partition capacity is available. It changes scaling demand, not the Event Hub partition count supplied in this topology.

Adjust liveness initial delay to accommodate measured normal model initialization. — The probe unit recommends tuning initialDelaySeconds for real startup behavior. Giving normal initialization time addresses the observed premature liveness restart without weakening steady-state readiness.

Change readiness to report success only when inference can be served. — Readiness decides whether a replica may receive traffic. The probe unit requires success only after the service is genuinely ready, not merely after its listener starts.

Change only readiness timing and keep the early liveness restart behavior. — Readiness timing can protect traffic during startup when liveness is already appropriate. Here leaving the observed liveness failure unchanged still interrupts loading.

Change only liveness timing and retain listener-start readiness success. — Liveness tuning can prevent premature restarts. It is sufficient when readiness already reflects application availability, but this explicitly premature readiness still routes inference too early.

Change the Service selector and leave the Deployment’s image and replica fields unchanged. — Changing a Service selector adjusts which labeled Pods receive traffic and can repair routing. It does not declare a new image or desired Deployment replica count.

Set the Deployment template image to v2 and spec.replicas to 3, apply the manifest, then verify readiness. — The manifest units place the image in the Pod template and desired count in spec.replicas. Applying that declared state lets Kubernetes reconcile replacements; readiness must be checked after asynchronous submission.

Restart Pods while retaining the v1, two-replica Deployment manifest. — Restarting Pods can refresh startup-consumed configuration after ConfigMap or Secret changes. Retaining this Deployment still declares v1 and two replicas, not the new release.

LOG_LEVEL: valueFrom.configMapKeyRef with name app-settings and key LOG_LEVEL — The ConfigMap unit demonstrates configMapKeyRef for one nonsensitive key. Its kind, resource name and key match the existing LOG_LEVEL source.

TOKEN: valueFrom.secretKeyRef with name api-credentials and key TOKEN — The Secrets unit demonstrates secretKeyRef for a Secret key. Its kind, resource name and key match the existing TOKEN source without embedding the value.

LOG_LEVEL: valueFrom.secretKeyRef with name app-settings and key LOG_LEVEL — secretKeyRef is valid when that name/key exists in a Secret, for example confidential configuration. Here app-settings is explicitly a ConfigMap, not a Secret.

TOKEN: valueFrom.configMapKeyRef with name api-credentials and key TOKEN — configMapKeyRef is valid for an existing ConfigMap containing nonsensitive data. The supplied api-credentials resource is a Secret; this alternative neither changes its kind nor reads it.

Change targetPort from 9000 to 8080. — The Service unit distinguishes the client port from the destination application targetPort. This matches the healthy listener while retaining the client’s 8443 port.

Change port from 8443 to 8080 and keep targetPort=9000. — This maps clients on 8080 to an application on 9000, useful only under that different client/listener contract. Both conflict with the supplied requirements.
Change targetPort from 9000 to 8443. — This would be valid for Pods listening on 8443 behind the same Service port. These Pods instead listen on 8080, so the mismatch remains.

kubectl describe service text-api -n ai-workloads — Service description supplies routing selectors, ports and endpoints. It is useful for connectivity configuration, not application output from the terminated container instance.

kubectl describe node worker-node — Node description helps scheduling and capacity investigations. Successful scheduling and pulls make it less targeted than the available previous-container logs for this startup failure.

kubectl logs text-api-pod -n ai-workloads --previous — The deploy/verify unit explicitly uses --previous for logs from prior crashes. The namespace and Pod name target the supplied single-container workload.

Retain the selector, change the Service port and check DNS again. — Changing ports fits a proven forwarding mismatch, while DNS checks establish name resolution. Neither makes the unmatched selector choose the required Ready Pods.

Set the Service selector to app=text-api, inspect EndpointSlices and send a request through the Service. — The Service and connectivity units connect selectors to Pod labels and EndpointSlice membership. The change selects the intended Pods, and the follow-up validates addresses plus actual routing.

Change the Deployment Pod labels to app=text-service and replace the Pods. — Changing template labels is a documented way to align a Service when that change is permitted. Here Deployment labels are explicitly fixed, so the Service-side repair is required.

Lower each memory limit from 6 GiB to 5 GiB while retaining the 4 GiB request. — A lower limit can constrain maximum consumption when a workload fits within that bound. Scheduling still uses the unchanged 4 GiB request, which exceeds each node’s available 3 GiB.

Provide nodes with at least 4 GiB of available request capacity for each needed Pod. — The Deployment unit explains requests as the scheduling input and the diagnostic unit recommends adding capacity when exhausted. Per-Pod requests must fit a node; summing spare memory across separate nodes does not place a 4 GiB Pod.

Reduce the Deployment to one replica while leaving node capacity and requests unchanged. — Reducing replicas can relieve aggregate capacity pressure when an individual Pod fits. Here even one 4 GiB Pod cannot fit either node’s 3 GiB remaining request capacity.

Restart A only and wait for B’s subPath file to refresh. — Restarting A refreshes its startup environment. Waiting would fit B if it used an ordinary updating volume, but the ConfigMap unit explicitly excludes subPath from automatic updates.

Restart B only and wait for A’s process environment to refresh. — Restarting B refreshes its mount. Waiting would fit an ordinary updating file consumer, not A’s startup-only environment variables, which do not automatically update.

Restart A and B; leave C running. — The ConfigMap unit distinguishes nonrefreshing environment values and subPath mounts from ordinary updating volumes. New Pods receive the current configuration; C has already observed the file update and rereads it.

Wait for all three consumers without restarting Pods. — Waiting is appropriate for ordinary ConfigMap volume consumers that reread updated files. It does not satisfy the two nonrefreshing consumption modes explicitly used by A and B.

kubectl describe secret api-credentials — The Secrets unit specifically uses describe secret to inspect metadata and existing keys without exposing actual secret values. Run it in the correct namespace or add the appropriate namespace flag.
kubectl get secrets — Listing Secrets shows names, types and data counts. This is useful for inventory but does not show whether the specific TOKEN key exists.

kubectl describe deployment text-api — Deployment description verifies the template’s requested secretKeyRef. It is useful for checking the consumer reference, not confirming that the referenced key actually exists in the Secret resource.

Repeat the request through the same localhost port-forward. — Port-forwarding is useful for isolated access to the Service or a Pod. Repeating it checks the tunnel path again, not the public hostname, ingress host/path mapping or external route.

Inspect the ingress address and host/path backend mapping, then request the expected public route from an external client. — The connectivity unit separately verifies ingress rules, assigned external addresses and requests from the client path. This tests the public route required by the gate rather than only the local tunnel.

Check that the Deployment still has the expected number of Ready Pods. — Readiness is necessary rollout evidence and useful for detecting workload failures. It does not prove the configured external ingress route reaches those Pods.
kubectl logs worker-0 -c api -n staging — This selects the application container but in staging. It is appropriate for staging application diagnosis, not the supplied production incident.
kubectl logs worker-0 -c proxy -n production — This selects the production Pod’s proxy. It is appropriate for proxy diagnostics, not the application container output requested.

kubectl logs worker-0 -c api -n production — The monitoring unit documents namespace selection with -n and container selection with -c. Both identify the production application rather than relying on the context default.
